content.content:
# The report and the record

## What every report holds

Your brief says where your report goes: a file that it names, your final message, or both. If it names no file, your report is your final message.

A finding is something that your work learned about the tree or the language, and that the record does not hold yet. Examples: a defect, a behaviour that departs from the specification or from a decision of the curator, a measurement. What you did along the way is not a finding, for example the files that you read or edited. Your transcript keeps that.

A fact is a finding that is an established property of the tree, the language, the library or their tools, and that later work builds on. A defect also gets its ledger row, and a fact about it may cite the row.

A point to report is a kind of change or finding that the curator wants to review. Your brief names its points to report. Examples: a changed line of a test that the team wrote, a checker edit inside a change to the library, a changed line of the model program.

Put each of these that you have in your report, in this form, whatever else your brief asks for:

- **Defects.** Each defect that you measured, and the test or ledger row that records it (`tests-writing.md`, "How a defect is recorded").
- **Sentences of the specification made false.** Each sentence of the specification that your change makes false, quoted with its file and line. Such a sentence says what walk or the compiled path does. It is in the effect of an Appendix I entry (`Specification/appendices/changes.tex`), or in a `\revision` or `\note{}` box beside a passage.
- **Decisions.** Each choice that you made among alternatives, as a decision apart from the findings: what you chose, the alternatives, and the evidence, cited. If no decision of the curator covers it, say so, and say which reading you acted on. A decision left as a line inside the findings counts as not made.
- **Points to report.** Each point that your brief names and the work reached, with its evidence, also one that only part of the work reached.
- **For FACTS.** Each fact that your work established, in the hand-over form of "Writing to the record". If your brief let you write FACTS, give instead the number of each entry that you added or rewrote. If your work established no fact, write "none".
- **Commands.** Each command that you had to work out because this skill does not give it, with what it does.
- **Questions for the curator.** If something needs the curator's decision, list it as a decision not taken, in the form that `exploring.md` gives. The reader of your report brings it to the curator. Do not choose which of your items anyone reviews.

## At a point to report

- If the work reaches a point to report, do what the brief says for it. For example, a brief can say that a defect in the code is recorded in a ledger row and not repaired.
- Then finish the work.
- If a step cannot be undone, or would change a decision of the curator, report it instead. List it as a decision not taken, with its alternatives.

## Timings and citations

- If you take a timing that you will keep, run nothing else beside it. All agents of the session share the machine's cores (the `cloud-container` skill).
- Name the machine with every timing: `nproc`, the CPU's model and MHz, the load at start, the JDK, `FORTRESS_THREADS`. Only a pair of timings taken in one run measures a difference.
- If you take a measurement again because the code changed, say what changed.
- In a report, cite the tree at file:line, and quote results, two to five lines, each with its command. Never cite a file under `tmp/`.

## POSITIONS and FACTS

POSITIONS and FACTS describe the present: no dates, no names of who found what, no "corrected" or "superseded" notes. The history of each entry is in `POSITIONS-history.md` and `FACTS-history.md`, beside them. When your work needs the detail of an entry, print the report section that it cites (`$T 'doc:PATH#HEADING'`, below). Read its history only when the tree disagrees with the entry.

Each entry is one line that starts with its permanent number: `F-87` in FACTS, `P-48` in POSITIONS. A FACTS entry is the fact as it stands now, what it means for the work, and the test that fails if the fact stops holding, under a bold title. If no test checks the fact, the entry gives the command and the output that show it. It points to the report section that holds the detail. Cite an entry by its number. If the reader must know what the entry says without printing it, add the first words of its title in quotes: F-87, "The first words ...".

## The gap ledger

The ledger's rows are the bug reports that the work fixes. A fix of a row starts with its reproduction, written as a test (`tests-writing.md`).

A row is one line of eight cells, at most 1,200 characters, in the table of a topic section. Reports cite a row by its number, which it keeps for good. A new issue gets a new row.

- Its status is one of seven words: `POSITIVE-VERIFIED`, `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`, `NEGATIVE-BOUNDED`, `CONTESTED`, `RETIRED`, `FIXED`, `DUPLICATE`. The last three close a row. The row template (below) defines each.
- Its class is a kind and an area, such as `implementation gap (checker)`.
- The earlier text of a changed row is in `explorations/fortress-gap-ledger-history.md`.

Read the ledger only through the queries below: it is too large to read whole.

A row states its gap as it stands now. A note adds a fact. If your work changes what a row says, write the row's whole new line with `rewrite` (below), not a note that tells the repair.

The heading reader of `ledger.py` does not expand the specification's `\Trait{X}` macro. So a row that names a library trait's section cites `Specification-1.0-frozen/` by line.

## Reading the record

Read only the slice of the record that you need. This tool prints whole entries, in parts of bounded size:

    T=explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh

- `$T 'F-87'` prints one entry by its number, and `$T 'P-48'` one of POSITIONS. `$T 'F-87+'` adds each entry that F-87 cites by its number, and each entry that cites F-87. `$T 'history:F-87'` prints its history. Run one when your brief or a note cites an entry by its number.
- `$T 'positions:WORDS OF A TITLE'` prints one of the curator's decisions. Run it before you choose among ways to do something. If several titles hold the words, it names them.
- `$T 'WORDS OF A TITLE'` prints each FACTS entry whose bold title holds them, and `$T 'section:HEADING'` every entry of a FACTS section. Run one before you investigate a behaviour of the tree, and when your brief or a note names an entry. These queries and `positions:` read titles only: before you write that the record does not hold something, also grep FACTS and POSITIONS for its words.
- `$T 'index:WORDS'` prints the INDEX lines that hold the words. Run it to find the notes on a topic.
- `$T 'ledger-find:WORDS'` prints one line for each ledger row that holds every word. Run it when you meet a defect, before you investigate it.
- `$T 'ledger:ROW'` prints one row whole. Run it for each row that you need from a find, your brief or a note.
- `$T 'doc:PATH#HEADING'` prints a section of any note, or of a `.tex` chapter, and `$T 'map:FILE#HEADING'` a section of a note under `explorations/coordinator/map/`. Run one when your brief or a note names a section. `#HEADING@WORDS` prints only the table rows and list items of that section that hold every one of WORDS.
- `$T --check QUERY ...` prints only where each query matches and its size. Run it before a query whose size you do not know. `--part N` prints part N of a long output, and `--help` gives the rest.

A word of a query that ends in `*` matches the start of a word. Any other word matches a whole word.

Before you edit a file of the original tree, list the ledger rows that cite it, and read each row that your edit can change:

    python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py find --cites FILE

## Writing to the record

- Write FACTS and POSITIONS only with `explorations/coordinator/tools/record.py`, never by hand. `add` gives a new entry its number, and `set` rewrites an entry. The tool writes the entry to `FACTS.md` or `POSITIONS.md`, and its earlier text to the history file beside it. It commits nothing: commit both files in one commit. Its header gives its usage.
- If your brief lets you write FACTS, add each fact as a new entry in the section of its topic, in the commit that establishes it. Put its detail in a section of your report: the file:line citations, the commands with their output, and the measured numbers. Point the entry to that section, by your report's file and the section's heading. If your report is only your final message, hand the fact over instead. Spend no effort on the entry's wording: it is rewritten to the record's form after your work.
- If your brief does not let you write FACTS, hand each fact over in the "For FACTS" item of your report, with:
  - the fact as it stands now, in one sentence;
  - what it means for the work;
  - the number that a decision rests on, if any, with what it counts; if its parts belong to different ledger rows, the part of each row;
  - the test that fails if the fact stops holding, or the command and the output that show it;
  - the section of your report that holds the detail.
- If your brief lets you write FACTS, rewrite a wrong entry in place. Otherwise say in your hand-over that the entry is wrong, with the evidence.
- POSITIONS holds each of the curator's decisions, in one place. Everything else points there. Write a decision there only if your brief gives it to you to record. If you have evidence against one, do as `exploring.md` says.
- Put new files of the work under `explorations/`. If you add a note directly in `explorations/` or `explorations/reviews/`, add its line to INDEX: ``- `PATH`: `` and the first sentence of the note's header comment.

Write the gap ledger only with `ledger.py`, which checks each line that it writes against the row template.

    L="python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py"

To add a row:

1. Print the row template, about 3 KB: `$T 'doc:explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md#The row template'`.
2. Write the row as one line in a file under your tree's `tmp/`, with `?` in its number cell.
3. Run `$L add FILE --section TITLE`. It numbers the row and puts it in that section. If the row breaks the template, it adds nothing and prints each rule broken. `$L sections` lists the titles.

To change a row:

- `$L note N TEXT` adds TEXT to the notes of row N. It refuses a note that takes the row past 1,200 characters, or its notes cell past 700 characters. `$L note N TEXT --check` writes nothing. It says whether TEXT fits, and how many characters the notes and the row have left now and would have left with TEXT. These counts include the separator that the tool adds. It exits 0 if TEXT fits, and 1 if not. Run it before a long note, or before a note on a row near its limits. If TEXT does not fit, shorten it, or cut the notes with `rewrite` (below).
- `$L rewrite N FILE` replaces row N with the whole line in FILE, a file under your tree's `tmp/`, with N or `?` in its number cell. Use it to correct the claim, cut the notes or change the reproducer. The tool checks the line against the template and keeps the old line in the history file.
- `$L duplicate N --of M` makes row N a pointer to row M.
- `$L close N --commit HASH --test NAME` marks row N `FIXED`, by the commit HASH and its test NAME. Run it once that commit is in `HEAD`, and commit the close after it. NAME can also be a file under `explorations/coordinator/tools/`, or `none` with `--note REASON`. For a `CONTESTED` row, add `--settled TEXT`, which names what settled its question.
- `$L landing-check BASE` prints each problem, and exits 1 on any. Run it when your brief asks for it. It checks the whole ledger against the template, so a broken row that BASE already had counts too. The problems are a row that breaks the template, an `XXX` test deleted or renamed while a row that is not closed names it, a row that is not closed though a commit says it fixed it, and a FACTS or POSITIONS entry that disagrees with a row's status.

## The repository's history

- The repository is a 2018 fork of `sirinath/fortress`, a git conversion of the project's java.net Mercurial repository. Its trunk runs from 2007-01-04 to 2012-08-31 and ends at `a874948ac`, the team's last commit.
- The commits after `a874948ac` are the revival's. After the tag `sealed-tree`, commit `75cca6683`, the revival began to fix the team's code, test first. Before it, the revival changed mainly the build and the toolchain.
- `git diff a874948ac -- FILE` shows what the revival changed in a file, and `git diff 75cca6683 -- FILE` what it changed after the tag.
- If the commands above fail, run `git rev-parse --is-shallow-repository`. It prints `true` in a shallow clone, where these commits do not resolve. There, a copyright header of Sun Microsystems or Oracle, as in `Library/Format.fss`, marks a file that the team made, but not which of its lines the port or the revival changed. If your task needs those lines, say in your report that the clone is shallow.
- The conversion cut 146 parent links, so a `git log` of a directory stops at a cut and misses the team's earlier commits. Use `git log --follow` on a file, or compare contents.
- To find who wrote something, or where the repository's history after 2012 comes from, read `research/authorship.md` and `explorations/coordinator/lineage.md`.
- Commit `8fe1daa8f` copied a third-party port of the tree to Java 9 onto the team's last commit, `a874948ac`. Give its lines no credit, and name no author of it in any text that you commit. In a reconstruction of authorship, attribute nothing of it to anyone.

# Committing and pushing

**scratch**
: Files and folders that your work makes and `main` does not keep: logs, captured and raw run output, copies of tools, lists and private caches folders.

Your brief says whether you commit and push, and on which branch. If it says nothing, commit on your current branch, and push it.

## What to commit

- Commit your change, its tests, your report if it is a file, and any reusable script.
- Commit what you write to the record, such as a ledger row, with the work that it records. A row's close follows the fix's commit (`records.md`).
- A probe is a task of a brief that builds a change to answer a question and does not land it. Commit its change as a patch file, with its report and programs, in the `probes/` folder that the brief names, and no edit of the original tree. If the brief names no folder, commit nothing of the probe: give the patch's path and the report in your final message.
- Keep scratch in your tree's `tmp/`, which is gitignored.
- Do not commit `.claude/worktrees/` or `.claude/agents/`, which show as untracked in a fresh clone.
- Keep a copyrighted PDF or deck in `research/decks/`, also gitignored. Cite it by its Wayback URL. Notes on it go in `research/extracts/`: your own summary, with brief attributed quotations.
- Put provenance and rationale in commit messages and reports, not in source comments.
- Name a model by its tier (Opus, Sonnet, Fable) in any text that you commit, commit messages included. Never write its model identifier, the API's name for the model, which starts with `claude-`.

## How to commit

Commit as you go, each commit in one command that names its paths:

    git add -- <paths> && git commit -m "<message>" -- <paths>

- The command commits only the paths that it names. Other agents may have uncommitted edits in your tree. Leave them alone.
- If you renamed a file with `git mv`, name its old path in `git commit` only, because `git add` refuses a path that no longer exists: `git add -- <new paths> && git commit -m "<message>" -- <new paths> <old paths>`.
- Never commit a copied directory, and never use `git add -A`.
- Before you commit more than a few hundred lines, stage them and read what you staged: `git add -- <paths> && git diff --cached --stat -- <paths>`.
- If the commit edits the original tree, say so in its message.
- End every commit message with this footer, exactly, whatever footer Claude Code suggests:

      Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>
      Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01AmiXNpJxQ6TBwec4vJZHDB

  If your brief gives another session line, use it. If a commit that is already made has a footer that names a model, by any name or identifier, leave the commit as it is. Such a footer is not a defect: do not check for it, report it or list it.

## Pushing

Push after every commit.

- If you work on your own branch, push it: `git push -u origin <branch>` the first time, then `git push`. Your brief says how the branch reaches `main`.
- From a session in a cloud container, do not try to delete a branch on GitHub, or retry a refusal with another tool (the `cloud-container` skill, "Rules for every agent"). Removing a worktree leaves its branch. Ask nobody in your report to delete a branch.
- If you work on `main`, other agents commit to it too. Push only your own commits:
  1. Run `git log origin/main..main`. Your commits are those whose hashes your own `git commit` printed.
  2. If it lists another agent's commit, run the command again shortly: that agent pushes right after it commits. If the commit stays, push nothing, and say so in your report.
  3. If it lists only your commits, push the three refs with this one command, and wait for it to end:

         git push --atomic origin main main:claude/worker-brief-fable-vnnuv8 main:blinded-fable

     With `--atomic`, the three refs update together or not at all. Do not pipe the command into another command, since a pipe hides a refusal. A refusal shows as a line that starts with `!`, and as a non-zero exit. The platform rebuilds a lost container from `blinded-fable`.
- Push no branch that this section does not name, unless your brief names it.
- If a push is refused, push nothing more, and do not run it again. Report the refused ref and git's message.

# The base build, seeded worktrees and the old code

**seeding**
: Making a worktree with a copy of the build and caches of a built, clean worktree. `seed-worktree.sh` makes the copy and rewrites the paths in it (`SKILL.md`, "The caches").

**base build**
: Clean worktree at the base, built in place by ant, or seeded. Every other worktree is seeded from it.

**old code**
: Base's code, run from the base build with a private caches folder.

Once the base build is built, run its code only as "Running the old code" says, with a private caches folder outside it. Any other run writes into the caches that every worktree is seeded from.

## Finding or building a base build

- If your brief names a base build, use it.
- If not, look in `git worktree list`. Earlier base builds are at paths such as `/home/user/fortress-base<N>`. A worktree can be your base build if it passes three checks:
  - `git -C <it> rev-parse HEAD` prints your base;
  - `git -C <it> status --porcelain` prints nothing;
  - it holds `default_repository/caches/bytecode_cache/fortress.CompilerBuiltin.jar`.
- If no worktree passes them, build one at a path of your own, outside the main tree. It takes about 200 s: start the build and the library order detached, with the `nohup` line of `session.md`, "Long commands". `<base-commit>` is your base: the commit that your brief names, else your tree's `HEAD` when you start. Say so in your report.

      git worktree add --detach <base-build> <base-commit>
      cd <base-build>          # then set up the call as build-and-caches.md says
      ant compileAll
      # then the library order (build-and-caches.md), then this walk run, which warms walk's caches:
      bin/fortress ProjectFortress/tests/BooleanOps.fss
      git status --porcelain   # must print nothing: the seeding script refuses a base build that is not clean

If you check a fix against its old code, use a base build at the commit that the fix starts from. If a brief names the fix's base, the fix starts there. If not, the fix starts from `git merge-base <its branch> main`, or from the parent of its first commit on `main`.

## Seeding a worktree

A build, and a run of `bin/fortress` without a private caches folder, walk's too, write into the caches of the tree that they run in. So build and run only in a tree whose caches no other agent uses. Your brief says where you work. If your work builds or runs code and your brief gives you no tree of your own, seed a worktree of your own instead of building one. Then work only there.

Seeding takes about 3 s and 206 MB of disk. The new worktree runs walk and the compiled path right away, with the library already compiled.

    explorations/coordinator/tools/seed-worktree.sh <base-build> <new-worktree> <branch> [<start-point>]

- The script checks out `<branch>`: a local branch, else origin's, else a new branch cut from `<start-point>`, by default the base build's commit. With `-`, it makes a detached worktree at `<start-point>`.
- If the script exits 2, the base build is not built or not clean, and the script made nothing. Then make the worktree with `git worktree add`, build it yourself, and say so in your report.
- If the worktree already exists, the script keeps its branch. If it already has a build, the script keeps that too. `SEED_FORCE=1` replaces it.
- If you start in a worktree that has no build, seed it in place: name it as `<new-worktree>`, and its branch as `<branch>`.
- The script lists the library sources that differ from the base build's commit. Before a compiled run, take for each the step that `build-and-caches.md`, "After an edit of the library", gives.
- If the script warns that the copied build is the base's, run `ant compileAll`, then the library order. Without the warning, `ant compileAll` keeps the seeded caches.
- If another agent seeded your worktree, make the script's two lists yourself: `git diff --name-only <base> -- Library ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin` for the library sources, and `git diff --name-only <base> -- ProjectFortress/src ProjectFortress/astgen build.xml` for the warning.
- Reuse another tree's build or caches only through this script.

## Running the old code

If your worktree holds an edit and you need the base's behaviour, run the old code instead of reverting your edit. For example, see a test fail, or compare a program's old and new output.

`old-fortress.sh` runs the base build's `bin/fortress`. It sets `FORTRESS_HOME` to the base build and `FORTRESS_CACHES` to the private caches folder that you name, over your settings. Name a folder inside your worktree's `tmp/`:

    OLD=explorations/coordinator/tools/old-fortress.sh
    $OLD <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches compile P.fss     # the compiled path ...
    $OLD <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches run P             # ... then the run
    $OLD <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches P.fss             # walk
    $OLD <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches junit <worktree>/ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/X.test [Y.test ...]   # compiled .test files, in one JVM

- Any copy of the tool works, because it runs the base build that its first argument names.
- On first use, it fills the private folder with a copy of the base build's caches (36 MB, 0.04 s). Later runs use the same folder.
- Every cache file that a run writes goes to the private folder, and nothing else that it writes under the base build stays. So several agents can run the old code at once.
- Keep your programs outside the base build too, because a program writes its own logs beside it. The tool refuses a private folder inside the base build (exit 2).

To run interpreter tests on the old code, run the base build's `harness-one.sh` with `FORTRESS_HOME` set to the base build:

    FORTRESS_HOME=<base-build> <base-build>/explorations/compile-ladder/rung-inference-walk/harness-one.sh \
        <worktree>/tmp/old-harness <worktree>/ProjectFortress/tests/X.fss

The `run` step of a compiled `.test` is a separate `bin/fortress run` process. It inherits `FORTRESS_HOME` and `FORTRESS_CACHES`, and takes its class path from `FORTRESS_CACHES`. If you compose a harness run by hand with `-Dfortress.caches=<folder>`, set `FORTRESS_CACHES` to the same folder. Otherwise the `run` step fails with "Could not load ... Resource not found".

content.content:
# Running tests

**track**
: One of the five JVMs of `ant testFast`.

**shard**
: One of the four JVMs of `ant testSystem`. Shard i of n takes every n-th file of the sorted list, from index i.

**code state**
: Code of a tree as one edit leaves it. Only an edit of code makes a new code state; a commit does not.

## The two suites

`ant testFast` runs its tests in five tracks, four at once, in about 11 minutes:

- compiler: `CompilerJUTest` over `ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/` and `parser_tests/`. It is the longest track, so it sets the total time.
- library: `LibraryJUTest` over `library_tests/`.
- othercompiler: `OtherCompilerJUTest` over `other_compiler_tests/`.
- misc: the unit `*JUTest` classes, except `OneLibraryJUTest`.
- onelibrary: `OneLibraryJUTest` over `one_library_tests/`, with `FORTRESS_LIBRARY=one`. It starts when another track ends.

`ant testSystem` runs `SystemJUTest` over `ProjectFortress/tests/`, the interpreter's test folder. It runs its tests in four shards, in a few minutes.

`ant testSpecData` runs the specification's 130 extracted examples (`SpecData/examples/basic`, `preliminaries`, `advanced`) under walk, in about a minute. The gate runs it after the two suites.

The newest gate summary has the exact counts and times of the last landed run:

    git log -1 --name-only --format= -- 'explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-*/gate/summary.txt'

The two suites work in the same way:

- Each suite runs `ant compileAll` first, as every `ant` test target does, so it never tests stale classes. After an edit of Java or Scala, that build empties `default_repository/caches` (`build-and-caches.md`, "Building"). Each analyses or compiles the Fortress code that it tests, in private caches.
- Each JVM gets 768 MB, a 32 MB stack and `FORTRESS_THREADS=4`, whatever the shell exports. The run steps of the compiled tests get `JAVA_FLAGS=-Xmx4g -Xss64m`, also whatever the shell exports.
- Each suite deletes `ProjectFortress/test-caches` when it starts. Each JVM keeps its caches in a folder of its own under it, so that the JVMs do not overwrite each other's entries. Temporary files go to `ProjectFortress/test-tmp/`.
- The results are in `ProjectFortress/TEST-RESULTS/fast-<track>/` and `system-<i>/`, as `TEST-<class>.txt`.

To run a suite:

- Run one suite at a time in a tree, because each suite deletes the `test-caches` that the other uses.
- Read the verdict in the line before `Total time:`: `BUILD SUCCESSFUL` means zero failures, and `BUILD FAILED` means at least one. Every `ant` test target ends with these lines, and exits non-zero when it failed.
- To compare test counts, compare the sum of the four shards. A file added to `tests/` moves every later file to another shard.
- If a suite's count fell, a `.test` file or a `tests=` line almost always went missing.

## The switches that the harness reads

Put a `-D` switch on the `java` line of a run by hand; the `java` line in `harness-one.sh` is a model. On the `ant` line, it does not reach the suites' JVMs.

- `-Dtests=<dir>`: the folder that `SystemJUTest` runs, in place of `tests/`.
- `-Dfortress.suite.shard=i/n`: run shard i of n only.
- `-Dfortress.unittests.count=N`: run N files at most.
- `-Dfortress.unittests.seed=<value>`: the order of the files. Each run prints its seed as `FORTRESS_UNITTESTS_SEED=...`.
- `FORTRESS_JUNIT_VERBOSE=1` for `SystemJUTest`, `-Dfortress.junit.verbose=true` for the compiled tests' classes: show the output of passing tests too.
- `-Dfortress.junit.reset=false`: `CompilerJUTest` and `LibraryJUTest` keep their caches folder. Without it, they empty it when they start.

## Outside the gate

- `ant testNotPassing` runs the interpreter programs of `ProjectFortress/not_passing_yet/`, which are expected to fail. It fails if one of them passes.
- No suite and no stage of the gate runs the team demos, the programs of `ProjectFortress/demos/`. Keep each of the 52 demos that `DemoTests` lists reaching its end (P-79). Check them with the demo driver below, not with `ant testDemos`, whose test of the output is weaker:
  - If your change edits walk, the parser, a phase that both paths run, a class under `nativeHelpers/` that a `builtinPrimitive` string of the interpreter's library names (`interpreter.md`, "Natives") or the interpreter's library, run the driver once, after your last edit of code.
  - Print the driver with `explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'doc:explorations/compile-ladder/rung-team-demos/REPORT.md#Commands worked out'`. Save the first script that it prints, under "The demo driver", without the text around it, as `tmp/run-demos.sh` in your tree.
  - From the tree's root, after you set up the call, run `bash tmp/run-demos.sh tmp/demos`. It runs long, so run it in the background with a log (`session.md`, "Long commands"). It runs the demos under walk one at a time and writes `tmp/demos/summary.tsv`.
  - The driver's last line of output, before the log's `EXIT=` line, must read 'demos: 52 run, 52 reached their end'. A demo reaches its end if it exits 0 and its output holds no "fail" in upper or lower case.
  - If your change breaks a demo and you know how to repair the demo, repair it in the commit of your change. Otherwise, report the demo, its output and the ledger row that holds the missing feature, as a defect that your change makes or uncovers.
- Nothing runs these folders: `not_working_compiler_tests/`, `not_working_library_tests/`, `not_working_static_tests/`, `obsolete_interpreter_tests/`, `long_term_not_working/`, `linker_tests/`, `compiler_regressions/`. Put every new test in a gated test folder. A test of a defect that fails today is an `XXX` test there (`tests-writing.md`).

## When to run a whole suite

- The gate runs every suite once, on the tree that lands (`gate.md`). Your brief says whether you run the gate.
- If your edit changes the Java or Scala of the checker, of walk, of a phase that both paths share or of such a class under `nativeHelpers/`, run all the tests that it reaches. Run them once, after your last edit of code. The run needs no commit.
  - For the checker, run `ant testQuick`: the compiler, othercompiler and library tracks at once (below).
  - For walk, run `ant testSystem`. It is the same as its four shards run by hand.
  - For a shared phase (under `compiler/`: name binding, DSL grammars, desugaring, the marking of overloaded calls in `OverloadRewriter`), the parser or such a class, run both.
- Quote the verdict lines and the command in your report, with the commit if your code is committed.
- If the gate later runs on a tree that holds other changes too, that tree is another code state. Your run and the gate's run do not repeat each other.
- After an edit of the code generator (`codegen/`, `OverloadSet`) or the runtime (`runtimeSystem/`), run your own tests, and the four-thread atomic runs (`gate.md`) if `compiler.md` asks for them. Leave the whole tracks to the gate.
- After every other change, run only your own tests, through the scripts below, and the demos where "Outside the gate" asks for them. Leave the rest to the gate. This includes an edit of either library, though it reaches many tests. After an edit of one of the fourteen components that `OneLibraryComponents.test` compiles, also run `ant testOneLibrary` (`library.md`, "Designing a change").

The suites do not check these:

- the bytecode optimizer, which nothing in the compiler calls;
- DSL grammars, except one program whose phases the misc track runs: `syntax_abstraction_tests/ForUse.fss`;
- the linker's aliasing of apis;
- `fortress unparse`;
- the round trip of the `.tfi` and `.tfs` caches;
- a behaviour above one thread that one run of each suite at four threads does not hit.

If your edit is in one of these, your own tests are its only check. Say so in your report.

## One test, or a few

Each script and `fortress junit` below ends with the verdict of JUnit's text runner: `OK (n tests)`, or `FAILURES!!!` with the counts. Read the verdict there: the exit code is 0 whatever the verdict.

### Interpreter tests

Run interpreter tests (`ProjectFortress/tests/`) from the tree's root, after you set up the call:

    explorations/compile-ladder/rung-inference-walk/harness-one.sh <tree>/tmp/h1 \
        ProjectFortress/tests/X.fss [ProjectFortress/tests/X.test] [more files ...]

- It runs `SystemJUTest` with testSystem's JVM settings, at `FORTRESS_THREADS=4`, on a folder that holds only the files that you name.
- It keeps its cache in the folder `<scratch-dir>.cache`. It starts from that cache while the build and the library sources are those that filled it. Otherwise, or with `COLD_CACHE=1`, it starts empty. Its first line says `cache filled` or `cache empty`.
- It runs the classes in `ProjectFortress/build/` and builds nothing. After you edit Java, Scala or a parser grammar, run `ant compileAll` first. If your tree has no build, seed it or build it as `worktrees.md` says.
- Give it a scratch directory that holds nothing else. The script deletes the directory when it starts and when it ends.
- If a test has an `X.test` file (its keys for a refusal at load), name it beside its `X.fss`.
- It takes 15 to 25 s with an empty cache, mostly to analyse the library, and about 4 s with a filled one. Name several files in one call to run them in one JVM.
- It shows the output of passing tests too, and removes the Java stack frames.

To see the whole diagnostic, with its Java stack, run the program directly, from `ProjectFortress/` as the harness does, because an import is looked up in the current directory first:

    cd ProjectFortress && ../bin/fortress -debug stacktrace tests/X.fss

The direct run and the harness use different heaps (`interpreter.md`, "Running a program").

### Compiled tests

Compiled tests are the `.test` files in `compiler_tests/`, `library_tests/` and `other_compiler_tests/`. They link with the library's jars in the tree's `default_repository/caches`. If a build started the caches again, or the tree's caches are empty, run the library order first (`build-and-caches.md`). The tests of `one_library_tests/` compile against the one library, and a run test there needs the jars of its fourteen components. Run the tests in one of these ways:

- `ant testOneLibrary` compiles the fourteen first, with `OneLibraryComponents.test`, in its own caches folder, `ProjectFortress/test-caches/fast-onelibrary`. Each suite deletes that folder when it starts, and only `testFast` and `testOneLibrary` fill it again.
- With `junit.sh`, set `FORTRESS_LIBRARY=one ONE_JVM=1`, and name `OneLibraryComponents.test` first. The compiles write to `default_repository/caches-one`, and the jars stay there after the call. Its `FortressLibrary` alone takes about 135 to 160 s, so run the call in the background (`session.md`).
- For a run by hand against the onelibrary track's jars, set `FORTRESS_CACHES=<tree>/ProjectFortress/test-caches/fast-onelibrary` and `FORTRESS_LIBRARY=one`. The build does not touch that folder, so run `ant testOneLibrary` again after an edit of Java or Scala.

The script is `explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-N/merged-tests/junit.sh`. `climb-batch-N` is the folder's real name, not a placeholder. Run your own tree's copy: it runs the tree that it is in.

    ONE_JVM=1 explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-N/merged-tests/junit.sh <label> \
        ProjectFortress/compiler_tests X.test Y.test > <tree>/tmp/junit-<label>.txt 2>&1

- `<label>` is any word. It marks the run's lines in the output. The script writes to standard output only, so redirect it to your `tmp/`.
- With `ONE_JVM=1`, the whole list runs in one `fortress junit` run, in one JVM. The compile and link tests run before the run tests, as in the suite. Without `ONE_JVM=1`, each file gets its own JVM.
- It removes the named components' entries from the tree's `default_repository/caches` before the whole list and after it, not between files. So a link test and the run test that uses its jar pass in one call, with or without `ONE_JVM=1`.
- It runs the classes in `ProjectFortress/build/` and builds nothing, as `harness-one.sh` does.
- It removes the Java stack frames, and cuts each line at 240 characters.
- Its JVMs keep their temporary files in the tree's `tmp/`, and run at `FORTRESS_THREADS=4`.

To run the same list in one JVM without the script, and without its removal of cache entries:

    cd ProjectFortress && ../bin/fortress junit compiler_tests/X.test compiler_tests/Y.test

Run all the new files of one test folder together, in one JVM, as the suite does. A test that passes alone can fail beside others.

## One unit-test class, or one track

To run one unit-test class: `ant testOnly -DtestPattern=BitsJUTest`. It uses the tree's own caches and the shell's `FORTRESS_THREADS`.

To run tracks of testFast whole, run their target. Each target runs its tracks as testFast does, with the same JVMs and private caches:

- `ant testCompiler`: the compiler and othercompiler tracks.
- `ant testOtherCompiler`: the othercompiler track.
- `ant testLibrary`: the library track.
- `ant testQuick`: the three tracks.
- `ant testOneLibrary`: the onelibrary track.

content.content:
# The specification

Three folders hold the team's specification:

- `Specification/` is the team's text, as the revival revises it. It says what the language means, except where a decision of the curator says otherwise.
- `Specification-1.0-frozen/` is the unrevised copy. Cite it as "the Working Draft of February 2011". Only `fortress.1.0.pdf` in it is the 1.0 release. Leave this copy unchanged.
- `Documentation/Specification/` is the team's later restart, which they did not finish. If its Types chapter, `Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/types.tick`, covers a topic, cite it beside `Specification/` as the designers' later word.

Appendix I, `Specification/appendices/changes.tex`, records the changes to the text. Its revival section has one entry for each change that the revival made.

A draft build prints the team's `\note{}` boxes, and a release build hides them. Many say that a feature was not built, for example "Reduction variables are not yet supported." Before you record a missing feature as a gap, grep the notes of its chapter: `grep -n '\\note{' Specification/<file>.tex`.

The api listings of the library part are generated from the library's `.fsi` files when the specification is built (`Specification/library/apis/`, not in the tree). A listing shows the library itself, so it cannot justify a change of the library. Cite the `.fsi` file.

To weigh the specification against the team's later texts, or to find the designers' reason for a rule, read `exploring.md`, "Weighing the sources".

## Changing the text: the revision form

Every change of the text has the four parts below, so that no disagreement between the text and an implementation stays hidden.

1. An entry in the revival section of Appendix I: a `\subsection` with a `\seclabel`. The entry gives:
   - the affected sections, the change, its rationale and its effect. The effect names each departure: each way in which walk or the compiled path does not do what the new text says, with its ledger row.
   - the original text, quoted with its path and line in `Specification-1.0-frozen/`;
   - what a reversal to the alternative not taken would need;
   - the decision of the curator that it follows (its POSITIONS entry), or the reason that your brief gives.

   For the form, print one entry, about 2 KB: `explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'doc:Specification/appendices/changes.tex#choice of a coercion'`.

2. At each changed passage, a callout that prints in every build, unlike a `\note`:

       \revision{<label>}{<what changed, in a sentence or two>}

   `<label>` is the `\seclabel` of the entry. `Specification/fortress/fortress.tex` defines `\revision`.

3. The front matter's one paragraph on the revision, in `Specification/fortress/preamble.tex`. If your change makes it false, correct it.

4. The full reasoning, in `decision-record.md` in the folder of your work under `explorations/`: each changed passage, the original and the new text, the reason, and the way back. For the form, print one passage of an earlier record, about 4 KB: `explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'doc:explorations/compile-ladder/rung-spec-route-a/decision-record.md#3.3'`.

If the revision refuses an example, keep the example in the text, marked "Not allowed", as the specification itself does. If your change contradicts a calculus of Appendix A, keep the calculus's rules and soundness claims. Add a callout to it that says what it predates.

Check each changed sentence of `Specification/` or `Documentation/` against the curator's decisions. If it says what walk or the compiled path does, run a program that shows it.

## Building it

To check your LaTeX, build the specification in a built tree, after the setup lines. It takes about 90 s, so start it detached (`session.md`, "Long commands"):

    nohup bash -c '( cd Specification/fortress && ./ant genSource && ./ant tex ) > tmp/spec.txt 2>&1; echo EXIT=$? >> tmp/spec.txt' >/dev/null 2>&1 &

- Both commands must end in `BUILD SUCCESSFUL`, and `grep -c 'LaTeX Warning: Reference\|LaTeX Warning: Label .* multiply defined\|LaTeX Warning: There were multiply-defined labels\|^! Undefined control sequence' Specification/fortress/fortress.log` must print 0.
- If `pdflatex` is missing, install the packages of the `PKGS` line of `explorations/experiment/setup.sh` with `apt-get update -qq && apt-get install -y`.
- The build writes only ignored files, its log among them, which can reach 400 MB. Remove them afterwards: `git clean -fXq -- Specification`.
- Update `Specification/fortress.pdf` only if your brief asks for it: copy `Specification/fortress/fortress.pdf` over it.

## When the text and an implementation disagree

- If a decision of the curator says which side is correct, the other side is wrong. If the wrong side is in your area, change it to agree. If not, record the departure as `tests-writing.md`, "How a defect is recorded", says.
- If no decision says so, the disagreement is a conflict. Switch to exploring (`exploring.md`).
- If the passage has an Appendix I entry, name the departure or the conflict in the entry's effect, with its ledger row. Then the text claims no more than holds.

## Citing it

- If your change renames or removes a section that a test names, update that citation in the same commit.
- Inside the text, cite a section with `\secref{label}`.

# Climb batch 35: the gather's record

Written at the gather stage of climb batch 35 (2026-11-23), the first of the two runs of `explorations/coordinator/CLIMB-BATCH-35.md`, a housekeeping batch: each rung fixes defects where walk and the compiled path behave differently or depart from the specification, each closing its ledger row, test first. All five rungs were approved and landed: R (a numeral with a radix point keeps its leading zeros in its digit count), W (walk's subscript before a superscript, and its tuple binding run once), S (the compiled dispatch method of a functional method whose self is not first), O (the modifier `override` compiled, and the checker's refusal of one that overrides nothing) and A (an exit out of an atomic block keeps the block's writes).

**Preconditions.** `git status --porcelain` printed nothing, and `13f4fdea75` is an ancestor of `HEAD` (`git merge-base --is-ancestor`, exit 0). # Rung E's record lines, climb batch 35b: the logical equivalence of two booleans in the one library (row 184)

Commits on `wip/rung-boolean-equivalence`: `6ca6cee9f7` (the library edit and its two tests), `b37bc43aa7` (the XXX test of NEW-E-1). The detail of every line is in `explorations/compile-ladder/rung-boolean-equivalence/REPORT.md`.

## Findings

1. **The one library declares the logical equivalence of two booleans, `EQV` (`≡`, U+2261), and its negation `NEQV` (`≢`, U+2262), as top-level operators over two booleans beside `opr <->`** (`Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:2793-2794`, `Library/FortressLibrary.fss:4923-4924`). `EQV`'s body is `if a then b else NOT b end`, which calls no `=`; `NEQV`'s is `NOT (a EQV b)`, the specification's definition (`Specification/basic-lib/Fortress.NegatedOperators.tex:34-35`). Conditions: walk, and the compiled path with `FORTRESS_LIBRARY=one`; until the switch-over, the compiled path without the variable runs the prelude's own methods of `Boolean` (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fsi:465-466`). Evidence: `ProjectFortress/tests/BooleanEquivalenceWalk.fss`, eight cases, `OK (1 test)` through `harness-one.sh`, refused 'Operator NEQV is not defined.' on the base; `ProjectFortress/one_library_tests/OneLibraryBooleanEquivalence.test`, a compile test, `OK` in `ant testOneLibrary` (41 tests, 0 failures), 'Operator EQV is not defined.' and 'Operator NEQV is not defined.' on the base; by hand, the same program compiled under the one library runs, `PASS` (`FORTRESS_CACHES=$FORTRESS_HOME/ProjectFortress/test-caches/fast-onelibrary FORTRESS_LIBRARY=one ../bin/fortress run OneLibraryBooleanEquivalence`). What it means: a program writes `a EQV b` or `a ≡ b` for two booleans on both paths, also after the switch-over; the skill's "write `a <-> b`" (`.claude/skills/fortress-repo/references/revival-changes.md:57`) no longer holds.
2. **`EQV` on two objects of a program's own type is now a type error on both paths.** Under walk, row 184's program (`a ≡ b` for two `Pt(1)` of `object Pt(x: ZZ32)`) stops at the call, 'Unification error: Closure/Constructor for EQV param 1 (a:Boolean) got arg Pt of type Pt', exit 1, in place of the InterpreterBug; compiled, against the one library and against the prelude alike, 'Could not check call to operator EQV - (Boolean, Boolean)->Boolean is not applicable to an argument of type (Pt, Pt).' (`bin/fortress compile`, rc 255). What it means: row 184 closes; a program's type that wants `≡` declares it, as AplCore does (`explorations/apl/base/AplCore.fss:207-224`).
3. **Walk loads a program that applies, as a link of a chain, an operator that no declaration defines, and a call stops in `getOp` with an InterpreterBug** (NEW-E-1). Conditions: an operator that the parser reads as a chaining one, as the equivalence operators (`APPROX`, and `EQV` before this rung); walk only. Evidence: `println(a APPROX b)` for two `Pt(1)`, `bin/fortress UndeclaredChainOp.fss`, rc 1, '** bug! Expect all oprefs to be top level APPROX'; compiled, against either library, rc 255, 'Operator APPROX is not defined.'; `ProjectFortress/tests/XXXUndeclaredChainOperatorWalk.fss` with its `.test`, green as an expected failure ('Saw expected failure: loaded and ran, not refused at load'), red on a deliberate fix ('Refused at load as its keys name'). Mechanism: walk turns the chain desugaring off (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/Shell.java:286-288`, `:491-492`); the disambiguator checks an `OpExpr`'s operator (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/disambiguator/ExprDisambiguator.scala:498-503`) but not a chain's links; `forChainExpr` (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/evaluator/Evaluator.java:437-469`) calls `getOp` (`:893-909`). The specification settles it: a name not in scope is a static error (`Specification/basic/declarations.tex:416-419`). What it means: under walk, a misspelt or undeclared equivalence operator shows only when it runs, as an internal error.
4. **`seed-worktree.sh` copies `ProjectFortress/build` and not `ProjectFortress/build-one`** (`explorations/coordinator/tools/seed-worktree.sh:86-93`). Conditions: a worktree seeded from a base build that has `build-one`, before any `ant` target runs in it. Evidence, in this rung's seeded worktree: `FORTRESS_LIBRARY=one ../bin/fortress run OneLibraryBooleanEquivalence` stopped, 'java.lang.Error: The type ZZ of the library that the compiled path reads is not compiled over com.sun.fortress.compiler.runtimeValues.FZZ of the run-time classes on the class path'; the first `ant` target (`ant testOneLibrary`) printed 'Sources and build as the last build left them? no' and 'Scala classes up to date? no', rebuilt the Scala, and emptied both seeded caches ('Caches .../default_repository/caches started again, empty', the same for `caches-one`), since the implementation's stamp covers `build-one` (`build.xml:400-402`, `:469-470`). After it, the run printed `PASS`. What it means: the skill's "Without the warning, `ant compileAll` keeps the seeded caches" (`.claude/skills/fortress-repo/references/worktrees.md:45`) does not hold for a seeded worktree today; a seeded worker's first build costs a Scala build and the library order, and a compiled one-library run by hand needs an `ant` target first. A defect of a coordinator tool, not of the tree: no ledger row.
5. **The program over AplCore** (`import AplCore.{...}`, `FORTRESS_SOURCE_PATH` as `explorations/apl/rung-1/Rung1.fss:9-11`) prints, with a filled private cache, '1.0', '1.0', '0.0' for AplCore's prefix `≢ 3.0`, `3.0 ≡ 3.0` and `3.0 ≡ 4.0` (the base's three) and 'false', 'true' for `t EQV f` and `t NEQV f`: AplCore's seven infix `≡` and four prefix `≢` load beside the library's two. With an empty cache walk refuses at load AplCore's `<` over two `Array3` beside `StandardPartialOrder`'s `<`, 'fails the Meet Rule', which is row 342's cold-cache check (the APL experiments' `explorations/apl/gaps.md:158`), not this rung's.
6. **Neither stage moves:** the count on the final tree equals the last landed table (`diff` prints nothing; total 0), and the distance prints `DISTANCE SAME   0`, no site in `errors.tsv` (both on `b37bc43aa7`, the code of `6ca6cee9f7`).
7. **On the compiled path under the compiler's prelude, `≢` (`NEQV`) takes two values of any type and answers their strict non-equivalence, where the specification gives it only as `¬` of `≡`** (NEW-E-2, the skeptic's). Conditions: the compiled path without `FORTRESS_LIBRARY=one`, until the switch-over. Evidence: `Pt(1) ≢ Pt(2)` for a program's `object Pt(x: ZZ32)`, compiled and run on the base's code (`old-fortress.sh ... compile` then `run`), printed `REACHED` and `true`; on this rung's code walk stops at the call, 'Unification error: Closure/Constructor for NEQV param 1 (a:Boolean) got arg Pt of type Pt', and the compile under the one library is refused, 'Could not check call to operator NEQV'; on the base's code walk refused the program at load, 'Operator NEQV is not defined.' Mechanism: `opr NEQV(a:Any, b:Any):Boolean = NOT (a === b)` (`Library/CompilerLibrary.fss:71`). What it means: at the switch-over a compiled program that applies `≢` to values other than booleans stops compiling, as the specification has it.
8. **The parser reads the overview's ASCII shorthands `NOTEQUIV`, `NOTSUBSET` and `NOTSUBSETEQ` as operators that nothing declares** (NEW-E-3, the skeptic's). Evidence: `ProjectFortress/tests/NotEquivShorthandWalk.fss` with its `.test`, green through `harness-one.sh` ('OK Saw expected refusal at load'); a program applying the three, on this rung's code under walk, 'Operator NOTEQUIV is not defined.', 'Operator NOTSUBSET is not defined.', 'Operator NOTSUBSETEQ is not defined.'; compiled on the base's code, 'Operator NOTEQUIV is not defined.' The overview (`Specification/preliminaries/overview.tex:401-405`) gives them for `⊄`, `⊈` and `≢`; the operators appendix gives `NSUBSET`, `NSUBSETEQ` and `NEQV` (`Specification/appendices/operators.tex:452`, `:643`, `:645`), and the parser's alias table follows it. What it means: write `NEQV` or `≢`.
9. **The one library declares none of `Boolean`'s operators `⊕` (`OPLUS`), `⊼` (`NAND`) and `⊽` (`NOR`), which the specification gives and the prelude declares, and no library declares `majority`** (NEW-E-4, the skeptic's; sibling sites of row 184 in the files this rung edits). Evidence: a program applying the three to the four pairs of booleans, on this rung's code under walk and compiled under the one library, refused 'Operator OPLUS is not defined.', 'Operator NAND is not defined.', 'Operator NOR is not defined.', four each; compiled under the prelude on the base's code it printed `OPLUS tt tf ft ff FTTF`, `NAND tt tf ft ff FTTT`, `NOR tt tf ft ff FFFT`; `majority(t, f, t)`, 'Variable majority is not defined.' on all three. `ProjectFortress/tests/XXXBooleanOplusNandNorMajorityWalk.fss`, through `harness-one.sh`: as it is, ' OK Saw expected exception', `OK (1 test)`; with the four declarations in the program for one run, `PASS`, ' Missing expected failure ', `Tests run: 1,  Failures: 1`. What it means: a later rung declares them beside `EQV`, in the same form, or the compiled path loses three operators at the switch-over.

## For FACTS

- **The one library declares `EQV` (`≡`) and `NEQV` (`≢`) over two booleans, as top-level operators beside `<->`; walk and the compiled path under the one library run them, and a program's objects get a type error.** `EQV`'s body calls no `=` (row 994 is about `=` of two booleans, compiled); `NEQV` is `NOT` of `EQV`, as `Specification/basic-lib/Fortress.NegatedOperators.tex:34-35` defines it. The specification and the prelude write both as methods of `Boolean`; the one library follows its own form for the boolean operators (fork E1 of climb batch 35, P-37). Tests: `ProjectFortress/tests/BooleanEquivalenceWalk.fss`, `ProjectFortress/one_library_tests/OneLibraryBooleanEquivalence.test`. Detail: `explorations/compile-ladder/rung-boolean-equivalence/REPORT.md`, "What changed and why" and "Row 184's own program, and the other programs".
- **`explorations/coordinator/tools/seed-worktree.sh` copies `ProjectFortress/build` and not `ProjectFortress/build-one`, so a seeded worktree's first `ant` target rebuilds the Scala and empties the seeded caches, and a compiled run under `FORTRESS_LIBRARY=one` before it stops with 'java.lang.Error: The type ZZ of the library that the compiled path reads is not compiled over ... FZZ'.** The implementation's stamp covers `build-one` (`build.xml:400-402`). No test; the command and its output: `cd ProjectFortress && FORTRESS_LIBRARY=one ../bin/fortress run OneLibraryBooleanEquivalence` in a freshly seeded worktree, rc 1, the error above. Detail: `explorations/compile-ladder/rung-boolean-equivalence/REPORT.md`, "Defects, and their homes".

Its specification cell names the operators' entries where it read "silent", its class is the library's gap (walk's mechanism is NEW-E-1), and its notes name the prelude's declaration:

Expect all oprefs to be top level EQV', not a type error, and refuses `≢` (`NEQV`) before the run: the one library declares neither operator, for two booleans or for a program's objects | NEGATIVE-VERIFIED | library gap vs spec (library) | `Specification-1.0-frozen/basic-lib/booleans.tex:252-263`, trait `Fortress.Core.Boolean`, `opr EQV`; `Specification/basic-lib/Fortress.NegatedOperators.tex`, "Negated Equivalence Operators" | ProjectFortress/tests/BooleanEquivalenceWalk.fss | apl rung 1 | siblings: NEW-E-1. `≡` is a chaining operator, whose link the disambiguator does not check under walk, so `getOp` raises the bug (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/evaluator/Evaluator.java:893-909` at 5a59551554); `≢` is not, and is refused 'Operator NEQV is not defined.' The compiled prelude declares both in `Boolean` (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fsi:465-466`); against the one library the checker refused both, 'Operator EQV is not defined.' Workaround: `a <-> b`. |

Then close it, once the landed commit of `6ca6cee9f7` is in `HEAD`: `ledger.py close 184 --commit <the landed hash of 6ca6cee9f7> --test ProjectFortress/tests/BooleanEquivalenceWalk.fss`.

Expect all oprefs to be top level APPROX'; the compiled path refuses it statically, 'Operator APPROX is not defined.' | NEGATIVE-VERIFIED | implementation gap (walk) | `basic/declarations.tex`, "Reach and Scope of Declarations" | ProjectFortress/tests/XXXUndeclaredChainOperatorWalk.fss | climb batch 35b rung E | siblings: 184. Rung E (climb batch 35b): the one library declares `EQV` and `NEQV` over two booleans beside `<->` (`6ca6cee9f7`), walk and the compiled one-library path run them, row 184 is rewritten and closed, NEW-E-1 records walk's unchecked chaining operator with `XXXUndeclaredChainOperatorWalk`, and the seeding tool's missing `build-one` waits on the curator.

## Revival change

**The change.** The team's interpreter library declared neither `≡` (`EQV`) nor `≢` (`NEQV`): its boolean operators end at `opr <->(a: Boolean, b:Boolean):Boolean = a=b` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:4922` before this change), so walk stopped on `t EQV f` with an internal error, '** bug! Expect all oprefs to be top level EQV', and refused `t NEQV f` before the run, 'Operator NEQV is not defined.' The specification declares `≡` as a method of `Boolean` (`Specification/basic-lib/booleans.tex:252-263`) and `≢` as a generic top-level operator over `BinaryPredicate[\T, ≡\]` (`Specification/basic-lib/Fortress.NegatedOperators.tex:25-35`); the team's compiler library declares both as methods of `Boolean` (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fsi:465-466`) and a second `NEQV` over `Any` that negates strict equivalence (`Library/CompilerLibrary.fss:71`). The tree now declares `opr EQV(a: Boolean, b:Boolean):Boolean` and `opr NEQV(a: Boolean, b:Boolean):Boolean` as top-level operators of the interpreter's library, after `<->` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:2793-2794`, `Library/FortressLibrary.fss:4923-4924`), so `a EQV b` and `a ≡ b` work on two booleans under walk and compiled against that library (`ProjectFortress/tests/BooleanEquivalenceWalk.fss`; `ProjectFortress/one_library_tests/OneLibraryBooleanEquivalence.test`), and on a program's own objects are a type error: under walk at the call, 'Unification error: Closure/Constructor for EQV param 1 (a:Boolean) got arg Pt of type Pt', compiled statically, 'Could not check call to operator EQV'. The reason: the specification's text gives the operator to booleans ("returns true if both arguments are true or both arguments are false", `Specification/basic-lib/booleans.tex:256-258`), the interpreter's library writes all its boolean operators top-level over two booleans (`Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:2784-2792`), and the compiled path reads that library after the switch-over, where the compiler library's declarations go. Under walk, an equivalence operator that no declaration defines, as `APPROX`, still loads and stops at its call with the same internal error ('** bug! Expect all oprefs to be top level APPROX'; `ProjectFortress/tests/XXXUndeclaredChainOperatorWalk.fss`).

**Provenance.** Row 184 of the gap ledger; fork E1 of the batch record `explorations/coordinator/CLIMB-BATCH-35.md` ("Forks the batch takes", item 10: top-level operators beside `<->`, in the library's own form), within P-37 (the compiler's prelude gains no declaration); climb batch 35b, rung E. The skill sentence it makes false: `.claude/skills/fortress-repo/references/revival-changes.md:57`, "The interpreter's library declares it for no type, and walk stops on it (row 184): write `a <-> b`."

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""The record's tool: it owns the form of FACTS.md and POSITIONS.md and of
their two history files, and is the only way to write them.

An entry is one line under a permanent number, `- F-87 **Title.** Text.` in
explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md and `- P-48 **Title.** Text.` in
POSITIONS.md. A number is never reused or changed: a new entry takes the
highest number its file has ever used, plus one. An entry stands under the
nearest `## ` or `### ` heading above it, its section. Its title is its bold
opening, or where it has none, its opening words up to the first colon,
semicolon or full stop.

A pointer is another entry's number in the sentence that needs it, alone
(`It builds P-48.`) or with the first words of the target's title in quotes
(`It builds P-48, "A type parameter the arguments do not fix ..."`, or
`P-48 ("...")`). Quoted words must open the target's current title (`...` or
`…` marks words left out); when an entry is retitled, the tool rewrites them
in every entry that points to it, in the same call.

The history (FACTS-history.md, POSITIONS-history.md beside the record) holds,
under `### F-87`, one block per change, oldest first: one provenance line (the
UTC time from the clock, the kind of change, `from` each report section,
`commit`, `by`, then the note after a colon), and the line as it stood before
the change. The tool derives the kind: `added`, `rewritten`, `moved to "S"`,
`merged into F-n`, `F-n merged in`, `removed`, `noted`; the numbering wrote one
`numbered` block per entry. A retitle that refreshed other entries' pointer
words, or a merge that moved their pointers, says so in one more line of the
block (`pointer words refreshed in: F-12, P-48`).

A `noted` block, which `note` writes, leaves the entry as it is. It adds what
the entry's history lacks, such as the curator's messages behind a text kept

kind: `correcting the block of 2026-10-13 19:07Z`, or, where blocks of the
entry share that minute, `correcting the 2nd block of 2026-10-14 04:41Z`,
counted oldest first. The block corrected is never edited.

<!-- The coordinating session's boot: its one home is the `coordinator` skill's `SKILL.md`, "The boot"; how the session works, and how the record is kept, is the same skill (`.claude/skills/coordinator/`). -->

# The coordinator's boot

The boot is the `coordinator` skill's `SKILL.md`, "The boot". This file keeps no copy of it.
Every write takes a lock (flock on .record.lock beside the record), checks the
state it would leave, appends the history blocks first and then replaces each
record file in one step. A write is refused only for what would break the
store: a bad number, a pointer that does not resolve or whose words do not
open its target's title, a line break in an entry, no provenance (neither
`--from` nor `--note`; for a noted block, no `--note`), a correction that
names no block or more than one, two blocks for one entry in one call.
Never for size. The tool does not commit: commit the record file and its
history together.

usage: record.py COMMAND [ARGS] [PROVENANCE] [--root DIR]

  PROVENANCE: --from PATH#HEADING (repeatable; PATH from the repository root
  or from explorations/, HEADING held by exactly one heading of it, as doc:
  resolves one), --commit HASH (in HEAD's history), --by WHO, --note WHY.
  Each write needs --from or --note.

  add F|P --section TITLE FILE   a new entry from FILE's one line, numbered
      record.py add F --section 'Landed semantics' new.md --from 'compile-ladder/rung-x/REPORT.md#The fix' --by coordinator
  set N [FILE] [--section TITLE] entry N rewritten from FILE's line, or moved
      record.py set F-87 f87.md --from 'compile-ladder/rung-x/REPORT.md#The question' --note 'cut to the form'
  merge N --into M [FILE]        N removed, M rewritten from FILE (or kept),
                                 every pointer to N made a pointer to M
      record.py merge F-90 --into F-87 f87.md --note 'one fact, two entries'
  remove N                       N removed; refused while a pointer to it remains
      record.py remove P-131 --note 'evicted to the coordinator skill, references/briefing.md'
  note N [--correcting TIME]     a noted block in N's history, N unchanged; needs
                                 --note; refused when the history holds it already.
                                 TIME: 2026-10-13 19:07Z, or 2nd 2026-10-14 04:41Z
      record.py note P-25 --from 'positions-audit/full/evidence/corrections-c1.md#History lines the tool cannot write' --note 'his message behind the text: 2026-09-26T08:01:03.475Z, ...'
      record.py note P-7 --correcting '2026-10-13 19:07Z' --commit b87a17de5 --note 'that block names bc8902f47, ...'
  apply FILE                     many changes from one file, all or none (below)
      record.py apply chunk3.md --by 'consolidation chunk 3'
  check [--base COMMIT]          the store's checks; exit 1 on a failure
      record.py check --base cc9424c2a

An apply file holds, in any order: `## TITLE` or `### TITLE`, the section the
new entries below it go to (an existing entry stands under no heading, or
under its own section's, or the `## ` one that holds it); entry lines as they
should stand, `- F-87 ...`, or `- F-?1 ...` for a new entry, its placeholder
replaced by its number everywhere in the file; `move F-87 to SECTION`;
`remove F-90`; `merge F-91 into F-87`; `note F-87`, or `note F-87 correcting
TIME`, a noted block. Each may be followed by one indented provenance line of
its own:
`  from: PATH, "HEADING"; commit: HASH; by: WHO; note: WHY`. Blank lines and
`<!-- -->` comments are ignored. An entry line equal to the entry is skipped:
to add to its history, write `note F-87`. A note whose block the history holds
already, all but its time, is skipped too, so a file run twice writes nothing
twice. One call writes one block per entry, so an entry is noted, or changed,
once in a file.

check fails on: an entry line without its number, or a line under an entry
that continues it; a number on two lines; a number with no `numbered` or
`added` block, or one gone from its file whose last block is not `merged into`
or `removed`; a noted block that holds an earlier line, or whose `correcting`
names no earlier block of its entry, or more than one; a pointer to no live
entry, or quoted words that do not open the target's title; with --base, an
entry at COMMIT that is neither its line now nor the earlier line of a block
in its history (pointer words refreshed by the tool aside). It reports, without failing: the entries over 600 characters, the
entries without a bold title, and the `--from` paths and the report sections
an entry cites (`PATH`, "HEADING") that do not resolve.

The reads are facts-extract.sh's: `F-87`, `F-87+` (with the entries it points
to and that point to it), `history:F-87`, and the title queries, which fall
back to the former titles in the history.

107:- To find whether a POSITIONS entry comes from the curator's words or from an agent's summary or default: the mining workflow. Its writer changes only a sentence that is false, stale or not the curator's. Run it on the entries that it has not traced, before the clarity workflow rewrites them. Its README: `explorations/coordinator/positions-audit/README.md`.
108:- To make entries read on their own, with their meaning kept: the clarity workflow. For FACTS, it first judges every entry by the six checks of "What an entry is", and rewrites only those marked reword or reorganize. Its README: `explorations/coordinator/tools/record-clarity/README.md`.
109:- To correct the entries that a review's findings name: the clarity workflow, with `findings.md` in each chunk's folder, in the form that its README gives. An entry changes only where a finding names it, and grows only by what the correction needs.
110:- To keep `fortress-repo`'s revival part short enough to read whole: the orientation workflow. Its update mode runs after each landing. Run its consolidate mode when a cold read or the regression quiz shows that the part no longer reads whole, or when an update cannot keep it within the README's budget. Conditions: only a comparison across trees, as with `old-fortress.sh`, reads so; the cause was not traced. Evidence: `REPORT.md`, section 5, second bullet. Meaning: compare a library's compiled output across trees only with both compiles reading their sources the same way.

# Rung E, climb batch 35b: the logical equivalence of two booleans in the one library (row 184)

- problem: walk stops on `t EQV f` with an InterpreterBug, '** bug! Expect all oprefs to be top level EQV' (row 184, `explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md:399`; the planner's run, `explorations/compile-ladder/plan-35/probes/fixes-35.md:28`), and the one library declares neither `EQV` nor `NEQV`, so the compiled path loses the prelude's operator at the switch-over (`explorations/compile-ladder/plan-35/probes/fixes-35.md:48`).
- spec: `Specification/basic-lib/booleans.tex:252-263` (trait `Fortress.Core.Boolean`, `opr ≡`, EQV) and `Specification/basic-lib/Fortress.NegatedOperators.tex:25-35` (`opr ≢`, NEQV, "applies ¬ to the result of ≡").
- precedent: the one library's boolean operators, top-level over two booleans, `Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:2784-2792` and `Library/FortressLibrary.fss:4914-4922` (`opr <->` at `:2792` and `:4922`); NEQV's body follows `opr =/=(a:Any, b:Any):Boolean = NOT (a=b)`, `Library/FortressLibrary.fss:98`.
- deviation: the two are top-level operators over two booleans where the specification and the prelude declare them as functional methods of `Boolean` (`Specification/basic-lib/booleans.tex:252`; `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fsi:465-466`), as fork E1 sets, `explorations/coordinator/CLIMB-BATCH-35.md:458`.
- deviation: `NEQV` is declared over two booleans where the specification declares `≢` generic over `BinaryPredicate[\T, ≡\]`, `Specification/basic-lib/Fortress.NegatedOperators.tex:25-27`; the one library has no `BinaryPredicate` (grep of `Library/FortressLibrary.fsi` finds none).
- deviation: `EQV`'s body is `if a then b else NOT b end`, the form of `XOR` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:4914`), not `<->`'s `a=b` (`:4922`).
- historical: `Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:2793-2794`, `Library/FortressLibrary.fss:4923-4924`.

One launch worked this rung. Base `5a595515546edc5564515d4492ff4d44b5d07153`, whose code is the base build's `0a83a70498` (`git diff --name-only 0a83a70498 5a59551554` lists only the record, the skill and `docs/`). The worktree was seeded with `seed-worktree.sh`, exit 0.

## What changed and why

Two lines in each of the one library's api and component, after `opr <->`:

    Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:2793  opr EQV(a: Boolean, b:Boolean):Boolean
    Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:2794  opr NEQV(a: Boolean, b:Boolean):Boolean
    Library/FortressLibrary.fss:4923  opr EQV(a: Boolean, b:Boolean):Boolean = if a then b else NOT b end
    Library/FortressLibrary.fss:4924  opr NEQV(a: Boolean, b:Boolean):Boolean = NOT (a EQV b)

The parser reads `EQV`, `EQUIV` and `≡` as one operator, named `EQV`, and `NEQV` and `≢` as one, named `NEQV`, by the alias table that `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/parser_util/precedence_resolver/Operators.java` holds, generated from `operators.txt` beside it (`EQUIV` at `:1250`, `≡` and `≢` at `:2107-2108`). `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/parser/Literal.rats:301-306` maps the same names only inside a character literal (`CharLiteralContent`, from `:198`). The specification gives `≡` on booleans: "returns true if both arguments are true or both arguments are false" (`Specification/basic-lib/booleans.tex:256-258`), and `≢` as `¬` of `≡` (`Specification/basic-lib/Fortress.NegatedOperators.tex:34-35`). The one library's boolean operators are top-level operators over two booleans; the two join them in that form (fork E1), and the prelude gains nothing (P-37).

Commits: `6ca6cee9f7` (the library edit, `BooleanEquivalenceWalk`, `OneLibraryBooleanEquivalence`), `b37bc43aa7` (the XXX test of NEW-E-1), and this report's.

### Why walk failed two ways on the base

`≡` is a chaining operator, so the parser builds `t ≡ t` as a `ChainExpr`. Walk turns the chain desugaring off (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/Shell.java:286-288`, `:491-492`), and the disambiguator checks the operator of an `OpExpr` (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/disambiguator/ExprDisambiguator.scala:498-503`) but not a chain's links. So the undeclared `≡` loads, and `forChainExpr` (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/evaluator/Evaluator.java:437-469`) calls `getOp` (`:893-909`), which raises the bug for the unresolved reference. `≢` is not a chaining operator: it stays an `OpExpr`, which the disambiguator refuses before the run, 'Operator NEQV is not defined.' The compiled path desugars the chain first (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/PreDisambiguationDesugarer.java:96-97`), so its disambiguator refuses both. In the analysed tree of a probe, not kept, the `≡` link's `OpRef` had `_lexicalDepth=-2147483648` inside a `ChainExpr`.

## The tests: the failing runs and the passing runs

- The edit is of the library only: no whole suite but `ant testOneLibrary` (above, `BUILD SUCCESSFUL`, 41 tests, 0 failures, `Total time: 3 minutes 34 seconds`).
- The ladder subset is empty. No first error in the baseline's `raw/` or the newest landed `explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-35/gate/ladder/ladder.tsv` names `EQV`, `NEQV`, `≡` or `≢` (`grep -rl -E 'EQV|NEQV|≡|≢' explorations/compile-ladder/baseline-2026-09-19/raw explorations/compile-ladder/baseline-2026-09-19/ladder.tsv` and the same over the landed table print nothing), and the ladder's drivers compile against the prelude (`explorations/compile-ladder/repair-r1-atomic-static/run-subset.sh:53-61`), which reads neither edited file.
- The demos and microGPT's checks are the gather's and the commit stage's, as the brief says. microGPT's components declare and apply no `≡` or `≢`: the APL program's `≢` is inside `apl⦇ ⦈`, which its grammar expands to `tally((r))` (`explorations/apl/mg/AplMgSyntax.fsi:255`).

## Sentences of the specification made false

None. `grep -rn '~184' Specification --include=*.tex` prints nothing; Appendix I and the two chapters hold no `\revision` or `\note{}` on `≡` or `≢` (`grep -rn -P 'revision\{|\\note\{' Specification/basic-lib/booleans.tex Specification/basic-lib/Fortress.NegatedOperators.tex` prints nothing). Outside the specification, the skill's sentence "The interpreter's library declares it for no type, and walk stops on it (row 184): write `a <-> b`." (`.claude/skills/fortress-repo/references/revival-changes.md:57`) is made false; see "Revival change" in `record.md`.

## Points to report

1. The declarations as written, and their place: `Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:2793-2794`, `Library/FortressLibrary.fss:4923-4924`, after `opr <->`.
2.
